name: Codex Argenteus
material: Purple-dyed vellum, silver and gold ink
maker: Scribe working in the tradition of Wulfila's Bible
description: The Silver Bible, a sixth-century manuscript of Wulfila's Gothic Bible translation written in silver and gold ink on purple-dyed vellum, probably copied in northern Italy for the Ostrogothic court. Rediscovered at the monastery of Werden, it came to Sweden during the Thirty Years' War and is now kept at Uppsala University Library. It is the most substantial surviving text in the Gothic language.

name: The Church Bell Against Storms
powers: Its ringing breaks up storms, drives away evil, and helps stop fires.
description: Swedish church bells were believed to protect the parish: they were rung to break up thunderclouds, drive away storms and pestilence, and even to help stop fires. The casting of a new bell was accompanied by rites, and the bells were thought to carry a blessing that evil powers could not withstand. Ringing against bad weather ('ringning mot oväder') is recorded in many Swedish parishes.
source: Swedish parish tradition of bell ringing against the weather

name: The Cat of Norrhult
description: A bewitched cat in a folk tale from Norrhult in Småland. In the tale 'The Cat of Norrhult', a cat behaves in ways that betray a witch's or troll's power behind it, and the cat's strange actions reveal the magic at work in the village. The tale is one of many Swedish stories of animals that are not what they seem.

name: The Cowbell of the Skogsrå
maker: Worn or carried by the forest spirit
powers: Its tinkling warns of the skogsrå's presence in the woods.
description: A cowbell heard in the forest in Swedish belief, and a mark of the skogsrå, the forest spirit who leads cattle astray. She is said to ring her bell or to ride a cow, and the tinkle of a bell where no cow is to be seen warns of her presence. The cowbell is part of the skogsrå's folklore as a seductive and misleading spirit.

name: The Church Keys
material: Iron or brass key and a Bible
maker: Church key, used by the household
powers: Turns or shakes to reveal the name of a thief.
description: The church key used in the Swedish divination called nyckelprövning, the key test. A key was bound between the pages of a Bible, which was then hung or turned while names were read, and it was believed the key would point out or shake at the name of a thief. The key-and-Bible test is documented in Swedish folk tradition for finding stolen goods.
source: Swedish folk tradition of the key-and-Bible test

name: Kirkebåt (Church Boat)
description: A long rowing boat shared by a whole parish to carry people to Sunday service, built clinker of pine or oak and owned jointly by several farms. Church boats rowed people across fjords and lakes until the early 1900s, carrying fifty or more parishioners at a time; surviving examples like the Rols from Stryn are kept and rowed again. Racing between parishes on the way home was part of the tradition.

name: Cauldron of the Underjordiske
powers: Lent by the mound folk, who always return what they borrow.
description: In Danish legend the underjordiske, the folk who live inside burial mounds, are said to borrow pots, kettles, and spoons from farmhouses, as when a mound-man calls 'lend me kettle and spoon, while I cook lamb soup under Kovsbakke'. They always return the loan, and breaking their bargains brought trouble. The motif is recorded in Evald Tang Kristensen's collections of Jutland legends.

name: Caduceus
powers: Charm of the herald; conduces the souls of the dead to the underworld; later sign of peace and commerce.
description: Hermes' herald's staff, first described as a rod wrapped with fillets or ribbons and only later twined with serpents; it charmed mortals and spirits and led souls to the underworld. Its winged form becomes the sign of peace and commerce in Roman retellings, recorded in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
source: Homeric Hymn to Hermes; later literary and artistic tradition

name: Arrows of Cupid
powers: The golden arrow kindles love; the blunt leaden one drives love away.
description: The arrows of Cupid in Ovid's Metamorphoses: the golden-headed shaft that kindles love and the blunt leaden one that drives love away. Apollo, struck by the golden, chases Daphne, who flees because of the leaden; the two arrows explain uncontrollable passion in Roman myth.

name: Corona Civica
material: Oak leaves (holm, esculent, or common oak)
powers: Rewarded a soldier who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground; granted lifelong honour and the right to sit with senators.
description: The Roman civic crown of oak leaves, second only to the grass crown in honour, awarded to a soldier who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground; the inscription 'ob cives servatos' and the right to wear it for life made it Rome's most coveted decoration, described by Pliny and Aulus Gellius.
source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History (Book 16); Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights (Book 5)

name: Chest of El Cid
powers: A ruse: sand offered as treasure to raise funds from the moneylenders Rachel and Vidas.
description: The chest of El Cid in the Cantar de Mio Cid, filled with sand, pawned to the moneylenders Rachel and Vidas as a supposed hoard of treasure to raise funds for exile; the ruse displays the hero's cunning and was never meant to be redeemed, a famous comic episode of the Spanish epic.

name: Caladbolg
powers: Legendary sword of Cú Chulainn, capable of slicing the head off a boar with a single stroke.
description: The famed sword Caladbolg, wielded by the hero Cú Chulainn in the Ulster Cycle, renowned for its sharpness and lethal edge. It appears in the tale of Ferdiad where Cú Chulainn uses it to cut the head off his opponent.

name: Caduceus
powers: Symbolizes negotiation and safe passage; restores harmony.
description: The Caduceus is the winged staff carried by Hermes, representing trade, negotiation, and safe journeys.

name: Claíomh Mór
powers: Said to bite through any armor or shield.
description: Claíomh Mór, the 'great sword' of Irish tradition, one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann carried into Ireland and linked with Nuada Airgetlám. Later lore gives it a blade that could pierce any armour or shield. The name is close to, and often confused with, Claíomh Solais, the sword of light.

name: Claddagh Ring
description: The Claddagh, a ring shaped as two hands holding a heart beneath a crown, made in Galway since at least the seventeenth century. The popular story of Richard Joyce, enslaved in Algiers, who sent one home, is late and unverifiable; older written records of the motif are scarce, so the origin legend is treated as tradition rather than fact.

name: Crown of Saint Wenceslas
material: Gold set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds
description: The Crown of Saint Wenceslas, made in 1347 for Charles IV and used to crown Bohemian kings. It is set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds and kept with the other Czech crown jewels. Legend holds that any usurper who sets it on his head will die within a year; it is shown only rarely and under strict conditions.

name: Cormac's Cup
powers: Shattered at a spoken lie and restored itself when truth was told.
description: The cup given to the high king Cormac mac Airt in Echtra Cormaic, offered by a warrior who proves to be Manannán mac Lir. It shatters when a lie is spoken and restores itself when the truth is told, allowing Cormac to test the words of his court. It is one of the moral test-objects of Irish wonder literature.
source: Echtra Cormaic (The Adventure of Cormac mac Airt)

name: Ceridwen's Cauldron
powers: Brewed the Awen, the drops of inspiration and knowledge, for a year and a day.
description: Ceridwen's cauldron in the medieval Tale of Taliesin, in which the goddess-figure Ceridwen brews a potion of inspiration for her son for a year and a day. The three drops fall on Gwion, who swallows them and gains the Awen before being transformed and pursued through animal shapes. The cauldron is wholly legendary.

name: Cinderella's Glass Slipper
powers: Fitted only Cinderella, letting the prince find her after the ball.
description: The glass slipper in the Grimms' Aschenputtel, the shoe lost as Cinderella flees the prince's ball. Because it fits no other foot in the kingdom, it lets the prince find his bride. Perrault's version makes the slipper glass; the object is a fairy-tale token and no such slipper survives.
source: Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen no. 21; Perrault

name: The Crook and Flail
aliases: Shepherd's Crook and Flail of Osiris
material: Gold and blue faience (mythic and royal)
powers: Signs of kingship and of Osiris's shepherd-care over the people.
description: The crossed crook (heka) and flail (nekhakha) carried by Osiris as emblems of royal authority and of the shepherd's care for his flock, laid crossed over royal mummies. Temple reliefs show the living pharaoh handing the pair to the god of the dead and receiving it back, and gilt examples were buried with kings such as Tutankhamun. Together they fix the image of the enthroned Osiris.

name: The Cup of Jamshid
powers: Reveals the whole world to the one who looks into it.
description: The cup of the legendary shah Jamshid, in which, according to the Shahnameh and later Persian tradition, the whole world could be seen as in a mirror, so that nothing was hidden from the king. The cup became a byword for far-seeing royal wisdom, and Persian poets used it as an image of mystical vision and self-knowledge. Its ties to the older idea of the king's divine glory are debated.

name: Cheonbuin
powers: Marks the royal mandate of the founder king
description: The heavenly seal that the Samguk Yusa says Hwanung, son of the sky god Hwanin, carried when he descended to Mount Taebaek with three seals to govern the world. Given to his descendants as the mark of royal mandate, the seal anchors the Dangun foundation myth in which the bear-woman Ungnyeo's son Dangun founded the first Korean kingdom.

name: Co Loa Crossbow
powers: Each shot could slay thousands
description: The magic crossbow of An Duong Vuong, its trigger made from the golden turtle-claw that Kim Qui gave the king at Co Loa. Each shot could kill thousands, but when the king's daughter My Chau revealed the secret to her husband Trong Thuy, the stolen trigger lost the citadel to the enemy.

name: Cuauhxicalli
powers: Receptacle of sacrificial offerings at the temple.
description: A stone vessel carved as a crouching eagle or jaguar, its bowl hollowed from the back, placed at the temple to receive the hearts of sacrificial victims; the name means 'eagle gourd.' The best-known example, the Cuauhxicalli of Tizoc, shows the ruler and his warriors. Spanish chroniclers and codices confirm its place in the public ceremonies of Tenochtitlan.

name: Chac Mool
powers: Receives offerings to the gods at the temple.
description: A reclining human figure holding a flat basin on its stomach, carved in stone at temple entrances across Toltec Tula and Aztec Tenochtitlan; the name 'chac mool' was coined by 19th-century explorer Augustus Le Plongeon. The figure served as a receptacle for offerings, linked in Aztec contexts to Tlaloc and sacrifice. Examples were recovered at the Temple of the Warriors and Templo Mayor.
source: Augustus Le Plongeon and later excavations at Tula and Tenochtitlan

name: Comal
era: From the classic era to the present
powers: Toasts tortillas and maize cakes over the hearth.
description: A flat, round clay griddle set over three hearth stones to toast tortillas, tamales and other maize foods across Mexico and Guatemala. Clay comales appear in Mesoamerican sites from the classic period, and colonial accounts describe the round hearth as the fixed center of the kitchen. The word entered Spanish from Nahuatl and the tool remains a household staple.

name: Calumet (Peace Pipe)
material: Stone bowl and wood stem, sometimes catlinite
powers: Binds treaties, prayers and peace in a single sacred act.
description: The sacred pipe of Plains peoples, its stone bowl and wood stem smoked in ceremonies of prayer, treaty and peace; in Lakota tradition the chanunpa was given to the people by White Buffalo Calf Woman. The name 'calumet' comes from French via early traders who witnessed its power to seal alliances. Carved catlinite bowls, the pipestone of Minnesota, are among the most famous examples.
source: Lakota oral tradition and early French accounts

name: Cedar Bark Basket
culture: Haida, Tlingit and other Northwest Coast peoples
era: Northwest Coast tradition to the present
powers: Holds water itself when woven tight enough.
description: Baskets and hats woven from shredded cedar bark and split cedar root by the women of the Northwest Coast, some so tightly made they can hold water and be used for cooking with hot stones. The weaving carries the distinctive twined patterns of each nation, from simple checks to complex animal designs. Cedar itself is the subject of origin stories tying its use to the forest's generosity.
source: Northwest Coast oral tradition and ethnographic collections

name: Coup Stick
culture: Plains peoples (Lakota, Cheyenne, Crow and others)
powers: Touching the enemy is the highest act of bravery.
description: A staff or lance carried by Plains warriors to 'count coup,' touching an enemy in battle without killing being regarded as the bravest feat of all. Eagle feathers and scalps added to the staff record each coup the bearer counted, a living tally of honor. Ethnographic accounts record that the four highest honors of Plains warfare were ranked, with counting coup above taking an enemy's life.

name: Lechuguilla Mask
powers: Worn at the Fiestas de los Santos Inocentes to escape King Herod.
description: The masked costume of the Fiestas de los Santos Inocentes in Hatillo, Puerto Rico, where on December 28 masqueraders run through town in vejigante-style masks and painted gowns to re-enact King Herod's search for the Christ child. Brought by settlers from the Canary Islands in 1823, the mask lets the wearer hide from the story's soldiers and turn the day into a chase of laughter.

name: Chiwara Headdress
description: The chiwara is a carved wooden headdress of the Bamana (Bambara) of Mali, shaped like an antelope with a long neck and horns. It is worn in pairs during field dances that honour the mythical chiwara who taught humanity agriculture. The vertical zigzag crest and pierced back recall the sun's rays and the roan antelope.

name: Chokwe Pwo Mask
material: Carved wood, pigment, fibre and feathers
description: The pwo is the carved female mask of the Chokwe of Angola, with a finely finished face, scarification marks, and a headdress of fibre and feathers. Danced at initiations and celebrations, it honours the idealised ancestress; its calm, polished beauty marks the grace expected of Chokwe women.

name: Chokwe Chief's Throne
description: Carved wooden chief's thrones of the Chokwe of Angola, with a seat supported by figures of ancestors, chiefs, and scenes of everyday life, often studded with brass tacks. The throne proclaims the dignity of the soba and the continuity of the chieftaincy; the supporting figures were personal emblems of the ruler.

name: Chipendani Mouth Bow
description: The chipendani is a small mouth-bow of the Shona of Zimbabwe, a curved wooden bow with a fibre string, played by plucking while the mouth shapes the tone. It is a personal instrument of young herders, and its light, rhythmic notes accompany the passing of time and courtship in rural life.

name: Chaoui Aures Kilim
description: Chaoui (Aures) weavings of Algeria are wool carpets and blankets woven on ground looms by Amazigh women of the Aures mountains, with bold stripes and geometric medallions in red, brown, and cream. Woven for the home and for dowries, the textiles carry regional motifs whose meanings are handed down in the weaving tradition.
source: Studies of Amazigh weaving (e.g. Ianthe Reswick)

name: Canopic Jar
era: Ancient Egyptian (Old Kingdom to Ptolemaic era)
description: Canopic jars are the lidded stone or pottery vessels of ancient Egypt that held the embalmed organs of the dead, each guarded by one of the Four Sons of Horus. Made from the Old Kingdom onward, they were buried with the mummy so the body would be whole in the afterlife; Anubis, god of mummification, presides over the rite.
source: Ancient Egyptian funerary archaeology; museum collections

name: Coolamon
description: Carved wooden carrying dish of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, shaped from the root growth of eucalyptus or from bark and used to hold water, food, seeds and infants. Scooped from a single piece of wood, the coolamon is carried on the head or under the arm and remains a practical and ceremonial vessel, often painted with the clan designs of its maker.
maker: Aboriginal craftsmen of the riverine and desert peoples
source: Museum and ethnographic records of Aboriginal material culture

name: Clapsticks
description: Paired hardwood percussion sticks struck together by Aboriginal singers and dancers to mark rhythm in ceremony and song. Known by regional names such as bilma in Arnhem Land, clapsticks accompany the didgeridoo and singing in corroboree, and each song owns a particular beat that encodes the Dreaming story it carries.
maker: Aboriginal craftsmen of Arnhem Land and the north

name: Cook Islands Adze (Toki)
description: Stone-bladed adze of the Cook Islands, ground from basalt and lashed to a wooden handle, used to fell and shape the timber for canoes, houses and carvings. The toki was the essential tool of the master craftsman, and finely made adzes were treasured and handed down, with the stone sources on the islands prized and controlled by chiefly families.
material: basalt stone, wooden handle, fibre lashing
source: Archaeological and ethnographic records of Cook Islands technology
